title: The ancient mystery beneath one of Powys’ most historic sites
description: Human remains dating back to the Bronze Age reveal a much older history beneath Pennant Melangell, one of Powys’s most atmospheric sites.

title: The story of the Black Country's secret ancient Greek Temple
description: Hidden among woodland on the edge of the Black Country is one of its most unusual historical landmarks, a building inspired by the glory of Ancient Greece and once considered a revolutionary piece of neo-classical architecture. Many residents pass close to the Temple of Theseus without ever knowing it exists as they walk the rolling hills on the fringes of Stourbridge. Tucked away on Wychbury Hill within the wider Hagley Hall estate, the structure has been described as one of Britain's most important examples of early Greek Revival architecture. The temple was built in 1758 for George Lyttelton, the first Lord Lyttelton, and was designed by renowned architect James "Athenian" Stuart. Stuart had recently returned from Greece, where he had spent several years studying and measuring ancient buildings in Athens. Rather than creating an entirely original design, Stuart based the folly on what was then believed to be the Temple of Theseus in Athens. Historians now know the original building was actually dedicated to Hephaestus, the Greek god of fire, metalworking and craftsmanship, something that would prove an apt representation of decades of Industrial revolution that were on the horizon. Historic England describes the building as a miniature replica of the sixth-century BC Athenian temple. It is regarded as the first building outside Greece and its colonies to correctly use the Greek Doric order, making it an architectural landmark of international significance. The temple formed part of the grand landscape surrounding Hagley Hall, one of England's finest 18th-century landscaped estates. The grounds were filled with classical monuments, follies and viewpoints designed to surprise visitors as they explored the estate. However, the temple's fortunes changed in the 20th century. The construction of the nearby A456 Birmingham Road separated it from the main estate, leaving it isolated and vulnerable to vandalism. Public access has been restricted for many years as efforts have been made to protect the historic structure. Today, the Temple of Theseus remains largely hidden from public view, standing quietly above Stourbridge as a reminder of Britain's fascination with the classical world. Despite being more than 2,000 miles from Athens, the remarkable Greek-inspired monument continues to overlook the Black Country nearly 270 years after it was built.

title: Ancient wildfires in the Levant may have inspired Neolithic pottery-making, Israeli study suggests
description: Pottery appeared in the region during roughly the same broad period in which fires, erosion and clay deposition reached their peak.
